project_type: Full-stack e-learning commerce platform (course catalogue, one-off purchase, recurring subscription)
project_description: A two-repository full-stack platform for selling textile-craft courses online. An ASP.NET Core Web API backend (EF Core, ASP.NET Identity, JWT, Stripe, Cloudinary) serves a Next.js 14 / TypeScript frontend (Redux Toolkit, MUI, Tailwind). Supports anonymous browsing with cookie-scoped baskets merged at login, one-off Stripe Payment Intent checkout, recurring membership subscriptions via Stripe Checkout and Billing Portal, webhook-driven state reconciliation, and an admin course-management surface with Cloudinary media lifecycle management.

backend_frameworks: ASP.NET Core Web API (net9.0 target, ASP.NET packages 8.0.x)
third_party_services: Stripe (Payment Intents, Checkout Sessions, Billing Portal, webhooks)

architecture.style: Two-tier: SPA frontend + REST API monolith with a thin service layer
patterns: Composable IQueryable extension methods for sort/search/filter (SQL-translated)

Optional single-container deployment: API serves built SPA from wwwroot via MapFallbackToController

business_impact.domain_fit_observation: Orders carry a required ShippingAddress and a delivery-fee rule (subtotal > 10000 ? 0 : 500) — physical-goods concepts that fit a generic e-commerce scaffold rather than either reading of the client's actual need.

engineering_challenges.title: Two payment models in one codebase
engineering_challenges.why_hard: One-off purchases and subscriptions have different lifecycles, different Stripe objects (Charge, Session, Subscription) and different reconciliation points, requiring three distinct webhook handlers each resolving a different local record by a different key. Getting it wrong means lost payments or unpaid access.

engineering_challenges.title: Subscription state owned by Stripe, mirrored locally
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Pending -> Active -> Canceled plus reactivation must be derived from out-of-band, possibly out-of-order, retried events. The handler distinguishes cancel from reactivate by inspecting CanceledAt and status together rather than trusting the event type.

engineering_challenges.title: Identity continuity across the anonymous/authenticated boundary
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Shopper intent lives in a cookie before login and a database row after it; the login path must decide what happens when both exist.

engineering_challenges.title: SQLite-to-PostgreSQL portability
engineering_challenges.why_hard: EF Core abstracts the provider but not its semantics. DateTime.Now values are rejected by timestamp with time zone, and migration histories are provider-coupled.

engineering_challenges.title: Operating a webhook that cannot be invoked locally
engineering_challenges.why_hard: Stripe signature verification requires a real signing secret and real traffic, so the handler can only be exercised against a live environment.

decisions.problem: Choosing an architecture for the client's brief
decisions.decision: React + .NET, agreed with the introducing technical lead and sketched on a client-supplied Miro board; .NET additionally chosen as a deliberate learning investment
decisions.reasoning: Collaborative architecture discussion plus a self-directed goal of learning C#/ASP.NET Core in depth
decisions.trade_offs: A bespoke two-tier build was heavier than the client's actual need, which a discovery conversation would likely have surfaced
decisions.result: Strong learning outcome, wrong tool for the client's real problem — the project's central trade-off, to be owned openly

decisions.problem: Next.js client and API are separate origins; need authentication
decisions.decision: JWT bearer tokens over cookie/session auth
decisions.reasoning: Stateless tokens avoid server-side session storage and work cleanly cross-origin
decisions.trade_offs: Tokens stored in localStorage (XSS-exposed); no refresh-token flow; 7-day lifetime cannot be revoked server-side
decisions.result: Works; expiry handled reactively by catching rejected fetchCurrentUser and redirecting to login

decisions.problem: Forcing registration before browsing loses conversions
decisions.decision: Anonymous basket in a 30-day essential cookie, merged at login with anonymous-wins policy
decisions.reasoning: Just-expressed intent is the live one
decisions.trade_offs: Basket is per-browser not per-person; merge discards the stored basket rather than unioning
decisions.result: Simple, predictable, explicitly commented in code

decisions.problem: Different payment flows have different branding and compliance needs
decisions.decision: Stripe hosted Checkout and Billing Portal for subscriptions; custom in-app card element for one-off payments
decisions.reasoning: Hosted pages minimise PCI scope and provide cancellation and payment-method UI for free
decisions.trade_offs: Hosted flow leaves the application's visual flow; custom element puts more responsibility in-house

decisions.problem: Catalogue edits must not alter historical orders
decisions.decision: Snapshot title, image and price onto order items at purchase time
decisions.trade_offs: Duplicated data; no foreign key integrity back to the live course

decisions.decision: SQLite in development, PostgreSQL in production
decisions.trade_offs: Provider-semantic drift only discovered at deploy time; migration histories do not transfer
decisions.result: Development convenience repaid with interest during deployment

decisions.decision: No automated tests; manual verification with deliberate ErrorController endpoints
decisions.result: Deployment-era commit churn is partly the visible cost

problems_solved.title: Lost basket on login
problems_solved.problem: Login replaces the browser identity, orphaning the cookie basket
problems_solved.investigation: Identified shortly after Identity was introduced (commit be3bc7b, 2024-08-30)
problems_solved.solution: Unified buyer identity behind User.Identity?.Name ?? Cookies["buyerId"] and reconciled both baskets inside the login handler

problems_solved.title: Unconfirmed payments
problems_solved.situation: An order is created before Stripe confirms the charge
problems_solved.problem: Treating creation as payment would grant access to unpaid orders
problems_solved.investigation: Designed alongside the Payment Intent flow
problems_solved.solution: Persist PaymentIntentId on basket then order; reconcile asynchronously in a signature-verified webhook flipping OrderStatus to PaymentReceived on charge.succeeded

problems_solved.title: Webhook handler crashing on unmatched events
problems_solved.situation: Stripe delivers events with no corresponding local record and payloads that do not cast to the expected type
problems_solved.problem: The first implementation dereferenced charge and order unguarded - a null-reference 500, which Stripe then retries
problems_solved.investigation: Visible as a hardening change made after the first implementation
problems_solved.solution: Explicit null checks returning BadRequest/NotFound before any dereference, in all three handlers
problems_solved.result: Unmatched events fail fast with definitive statuses instead of erroring into retry loops
problems_solved.evidence: Diff of PaymentsController.cs between main and origin/main

problems_solved.title: Orphaned Cloudinary assets
problems_solved.problem: Old assets remained in Cloudinary, accruing storage
problems_solved.investigation: Addressed when admin CRUD was built
problems_solved.solution: Persist PublicId on the Course entity; call DeleteImageAsync(publicId) on update-with-new-image and on delete

problems_solved.title: SQLite to PostgreSQL deployment
problems_solved.situation: Development on SQLite, deployment onto managed PostgreSQL addressed by a DATABASE_URL
problems_solved.problem: The URL is not a connection string; DateTime values rejected by timestamp with time zone; SQLite-generated migrations would not apply
problems_solved.investigation: Iterative deploy-and-observe across approximately 20 commits, 2024-12-14 to 2024-12-29
problems_solved.solution: Parse DATABASE_URL with System.Uri into host/port/user/password/database and compose an Npgsql connection string at startup, environment-switched; reset and regenerate the migration history against PostgreSQL
problems_solved.result: A PostgreSQL migration set (PG_BackToNormal, 2024-12-29) is the final state of origin/main
problems_solved.evidence: Program.cs on origin/main, migration filenames, commit messages
problems_solved.qualification: Proves the work was done; does not prove the deployment subsequently served users

problems_solved.title: Cross-origin failure in the deployed environment
problems_solved.solution: Moved the allowed origin to CORSSettings:AllowedOrigins configuration; likewise moved Stripe success/cancel/return URLs to StripeSettings:ReturnUrl
problems_solved.evidence: Commit e6526fb 'fix: CORS Error'; Program.cs and PaymentsController.cs diffs

problems_solved.title: The problem that was not solved: validating the brief
problems_solved.situation: The client supplied a competitor site to model and a Miro architecture board; the stack was agreed with the introducing technical lead
problems_solved.problem: Nobody validated the underlying job-to-be-done. The organisation's actual need appears to have been a listing-and-membership site with course delivery remaining on a third-party platform
problems_solved.investigation: Only reconstructed after the client disengaged, by re-reading what they had asked for against what they already had
problems_solved.solution: None at the time; the lesson was captured afterwards
problems_solved.result: Roughly three months of correct engineering against an incorrect specification; the work was never demoed
problems_solved.evidence: USER_ATTESTED, corroborated by the repository stopping mid-deployment with no demo artefact and by domain-model artefacts fitting neither reading of the real need
problems_solved.note: The most instructive item in this dossier

lessons: A reference site is not a specification — 'build something like this' describes an output, not a problem.
Demo in week two, not month three. An ugly clickable slice early exposes misalignment while it is cheap.
A technical intermediary is not a substitute for the product owner.
Silence is signal: treat a slipping response cadence as a project risk to escalate, not a scheduling inconvenience.
For volunteer and unpaid work, agree checkpoints in writing — a shared date creates the moment where misalignment surfaces.
Develop on the database engine you deploy on.
Use DateTime.UtcNow by default in anything that may meet PostgreSQL.
Externalise every environment-coupled value before the first deploy, not after it.
Webhooks are untrusted, unordered and duplicate-prone: null-guard payload and record lookup, re-read the provider's API, make handlers idempotent on the provider's identifier.
Client-side route guards are UX, not security.
Zero tests is affordable until deployment, then it is not.

cv_bullets.framing_guidance: List as a VOLUNTEER / PRO-BONO engagement with a non-production qualifier visible in the entry. Do not lead the CV with it if paid production work exists — it is a supporting entry evidencing .NET/payments capability and UK engagement history, not impact.
honest_outcome_framings: Engagement concluded before launch when the client's requirements proved to be for a simpler listing-and-membership site than the bespoke platform briefed.
Built to demo stage; project discontinued by the client before review.
Volunteer engagement; platform reached a deployed staging environment and was not taken to production.
do_not_use: Any claim of launch, users, revenue, transactions, uptime or business impact
'Production' as a descriptor for the hosted environment — use 'staging'
Any framing that attributes the outcome solely to the client

interview_stories.theme: Tell me about a project that failed — STRONGEST STORY IN THIS PROJECT
interview_stories.situation: A volunteer engagement to build a course-selling platform for a UK training organisation, briefed with a competitor site to model and a Miro architecture board
interview_stories.task: Deliver a bespoke platform for selling and delivering courses
interview_stories.action: Agreed a React + .NET architecture with the introducing technical lead and built it — catalogue, basket, auth, orders, dual-mode Stripe payments, subscriptions, admin CMS — deploying to a self-hosted staging environment
interview_stories.result: Before the demo the client went quiet and never returned. Their real need was a listing-and-membership site with delivery staying on their existing third-party platform
interview_stories.what_i_own: Validated the solution with a technical intermediary and never validated the problem with the product owner; proposed a demo only once the build was substantially done, three months in. An ugly clickable demo in week two would have cost two days and saved three months.
interview_stories.what_i_changed: Open engagements with job-to-be-done questions — where does this live today, who delivers it, what happens the day after someone buys, what would you do if we built nothing — and schedule the first demo before the first sprint.
interview_stories.evidence: Commit history ending mid-deployment with no demo artefact; the author's own account
interview_stories.coaching_note: Rehearse the 'what I own' paragraph — that is the part interviewers are listening for.

interview_stories.situation: The API ran on SQLite locally and failed on deployment to managed PostgreSQL
interview_stories.task: Get the API running on PostgreSQL without losing the development workflow
interview_stories.action: Identified three causes (DATABASE_URL vs connection string, DateTime.Now vs timestamp with time zone, provider-coupled migrations); parsed the URL with System.Uri and composed an Npgsql connection string at startup; reset and regenerated migrations against PostgreSQL
interview_stories.result: A PostgreSQL migration set is the final state of the repository
interview_stories.evidence: Program.cs on origin/main; commits 'fix: datetime to timestamp issues' x5 and 'fix: normal migration', 2024-12-29

interview_stories.theme: Integration with an unreliable asynchronous third party
interview_stories.situation: Payment and subscription truth lives in Stripe; the application mirrors it
interview_stories.task: Keep local state correct given signed, retried, possibly unmatched events
interview_stories.action: Built three handlers verifying the signature, null-checking the deserialised object and the matched record, and re-fetching the Checkout Session and Subscription from Stripe before mutating state; added a duplicate-SessionId guard; distinguished cancellation from reactivation by CanceledAt plus status
interview_stories.result: Handlers fail fast with definitive statuses on unmatched events instead of 500-ing into retry loops
interview_stories.evidence: PaymentsController diff between main and origin/main

interview_stories.situation: A user has one basket in a cookie and another saved on their account
interview_stories.action: Chose anonymous-wins: delete the stored basket, re-key the cookie basket to the username, clear the cookie
interview_stories.discussion_value: The alternative (union the two) is equally defensible; arguing both sides is the point

interview_stories.action: Enforced authorisation server-side with [Authorize(Roles="Admin")], issued roles as JWT claims, used client ProtectedRoute purely to avoid rendering unusable screens
interview_stories.result: Correct split between UX guard and security gate
interview_stories.discussion_value: Leads into honest weaknesses: tokens in localStorage, no refresh flow, 7-day non-revocable lifetime

interview_stories.situation: Solo build of both halves of a commerce platform over approximately 4.7 months
interview_stories.action: Sequenced catalogue -> basket -> auth -> orders -> payments -> subscriptions -> deployment
interview_stories.evidence: 83 of 84 commits; commit history maps onto that sequence

interview_stories.theme: Learning something new under delivery pressure
interview_stories.situation: Subscriptions were added last and required Stripe concepts not used by the one-off flow
interview_stories.action: Chose hosted Stripe surfaces to inherit payment-method management and cancellation UI rather than build them
interview_stories.result: Full subscription lifecycle including reactivation, in roughly one working week of commits

interview_stories.theme: Working with ambiguity and a remote stakeholder
interview_stories.situation: Requirements arrived as a competitor URL and a Miro board, mediated by a technical intermediary rather than the product owner
interview_stories.action: Built against that material without direct product-owner discovery
interview_stories.discussion_value: What you'd now insist on before writing code — written acceptance criteria, direct product-owner access, a dated first demo — and how you'd escalate a slipping response cadence rather than absorb it

portfolio_material.overview: A two-repository full-stack platform for selling textile-craft courses online, supporting one-off course purchases and recurring memberships.
portfolio_material.challenge: Build, alone, a complete commerce system: catalogue with real query capability, a basket that survives the login boundary, two fundamentally different payment lifecycles, administrative content management with media, and a deployment path from a laptop SQLite file to a managed PostgreSQL instance in a container.
portfolio_material.role: Sole architect and developer of the ASP.NET Core API; near-sole developer of the Next.js frontend.
portfolio_material.most_interesting_problem: Mirroring subscription state that Stripe owns - deriving Pending -> Active -> Canceled -> Active from unordered, retried webhook events of three different object types resolved against three different local keys, and distinguishing cancellation from reactivation by inspecting CanceledAt and status together rather than trusting the event name.
portfolio_material.measurable_evidence: Repository and code metrics only. No production metrics exist - present this as a built-and-deployed system, not an operated one.
what_i_would_improve: Develop against PostgreSQL from day one
Refresh-token flow with short-lived access tokens held outside localStorage
A webhook event log table with idempotency keys and replay
Integration tests around payment and basket-merge paths
Remove inherited shipping-address and delivery-fee concepts from a digital-goods domain
Structured logging and health checks before deployment rather than after
portfolio_material.context: Introduced by a former colleague from a previous volunteering engagement. The client supplied a competitor site to model and a Miro architecture board; React + .NET was agreed with the introducing technical lead. The author additionally chose .NET as a deliberate learning investment.
portfolio_material.outcome: The client disengaged before the demo. The platform was never reviewed or launched. Probable cause: a requirements mismatch — a listing-and-membership site, not a bespoke delivery platform, was what the organisation actually needed.
what_i_would_do_differently_process: Lead with discovery, not architecture — where do your courses live today, and what happens the day after someone buys?
Demo an ugly clickable slice in week two
Get the product owner, not only the technical intermediary, into the architecture conversation
Treat a slipping response cadence as a risk to escalate
portfolio_material.presentation_note: Strongest when the retrospective is the headline rather than a footnote. A polished build that shipped is unremarkable; a polished build that shouldn't have been built that way, explained by the person who built it, is memorable.

audit_limitations: No production environment ever existed; all operational claims are and will remain unprovable.
The frontend checkout predates the backend's subscription endpoints, so the subscription UI could not be reviewed.
The attested engagement duration (~3 months) conflicts mildly with repository activity span (~4.7 months).
The root cause of the client's disengagement is the author's reasonable reconstruction, not a position the organisation stated.
Line counts conflate hand-written and vendored/generated code; stated splits are approximate.
No issue tracker, written brief or client correspondence was available to this audit.
txs-bk local main is 35 commits behind origin/main; all feature statements describe origin/main.
revised: 2026-10-17 — updated with first-hand engagement context from the author

engagement_context.engagement_type: Volunteer / unpaid — the author's second UK volunteering role
engagement_context.how_it_came_about: Introduced by a former colleague from the TiiQu / Qutii volunteering engagement, who had moved on and later recommended the author to this organisation
engagement_context.client: Textile Skills Center — a textile-training organisation
engagement_context.brief: Build a web app to sell courses, modelled on a competitor site the client supplied; architecture sketched on a client-supplied Miro board
engagement_context.stack_decision: React + .NET agreed with the introducing technical lead; .NET chosen deliberately by the author as a learning investment in C#/ASP.NET Core
engagement_context.duration_discrepancy_note: Author recalls ~3 months of engagement; repository activity spans ~4.7 months. Likely self-directed learning/scaffolding before the engagement began and/or work continuing after contact lapsed. Settle before stating CV dates.
engagement_context.outcome: INCOMPLETE — client product owners disengaged before the demo; point of contact went on a two-week holiday and never made contact again. No demo, no review, no launch.
engagement_context.root_cause: Requirements mismatch. The brief described a bespoke platform to sell AND deliver courses. The organisation's actual need appears to have been a listing-and-membership site (WordPress-scale) with course delivery remaining on their existing third-party platform.
engagement_context.root_cause_status: Author's reasonable reconstruction, not a position the organisation stated
engagement_context.hosting: Author self-hosted a PostgreSQL instance — STAGING/DEV environment only, never promoted to production
corroborating_code_evidence: Repository stops mid-deployment-work on 2024-12-29 with no demo artefact
DATABASE_URL parsing and PostgreSQL migration work consistent with a real self-hosted instance
Orders carry a required ShippingAddress and delivery-fee rule — generic e-commerce concepts fitting neither reading of the real need

user_attested_claims.claim: Chose ASP.NET Core and C# deliberately as a learning investment and delivered a complete, deployable application in an unfamiliar stack — including Identity, EF Core, JWT, middleware, DI, containerisation and a database provider migration.
user_attested_claims.why_strong: Self-directed capability acquisition demonstrated by a working artefact rather than a certificate.

user_attested_claims.claim: Identified, after the engagement lapsed, that three months of engineering had been built against an unvalidated brief — and can articulate which discovery questions would have surfaced the mismatch and why demoing in week two rather than month three was the decisive missed step.
user_attested_claims.evidence_level: USER_ATTESTED, corroborated by the repository stopping mid-deployment with no demo artefact
user_attested_claims.why_strong: Self-aware post-mortem of a real failure with the engineer's own responsibility owned rather than deflected onto the client.
